lessons.title: Getting the house ready and placing chicks
lessons.html:
Getting the house ready and placing chicks

Chicks need a warm, clean house with feed and water ready when they arrive. The first days are very important. Good care now gives strong birds later.

Before the chicks arrive

  1. Check that the house was cleaned and disinfected.
  2. Spread clean, dry litter (wood shavings) evenly on the floor.
  3. Switch on the heaters early so the floor and air are warm when chicks arrive. Your supervisor will tell you how early.
  4. Fill feeders or put feed on paper or trays so chicks find it easily.
  5. Flush the drinker lines and set drinkers low for chicks. Check that water comes out of every nipple.
  6. Check lights, fans, curtains and the alarm.
  7. Put a clean record card on the door of the house.

When the chicks arrive

  • Count the boxes and chicks as your supervisor shows you.
  • Put chicks down gently near feed and water. Do not throw or drop them.
  • Take out empty boxes. Do not leave them in the house.
  • Write the date, number of chicks and where they came from on the record card.

Watch the chicks

Look at how the chicks behave:

What you seeWhat it means
Chicks crowd under heatersToo cold
Chicks pant and stay far from heatersToo hot
Chicks crowd on one sideDraught or uneven light
Chicks spread out, eating, drinking and restingComfortable

A few hours after placement, gently feel chicks' crops. A full, soft crop means the chick has found feed and water. Tell your supervisor if many crops are empty.

lessons.title: Daily care of the flock
lessons.html:
Daily care of the flock

Walk the house

Walk slowly through the whole house several times a day. Look at the birds, feed, water, litter and equipment. Calm, slow walking does not scare the birds.

Feed

  • Check that feeders are full and working, and that augers run.
  • Raise feeders as birds grow, so the edge is about at the birds' back height, as your supervisor shows you.
  • Report mouldy, wet or strange-smelling feed.
  • Check that the silo has enough feed.

Water

  • Check that every drinker line has water. Press a few nipples to test.
  • Raise drinkers as birds grow.
  • Fix or report leaks quickly; leaks make wet litter.
  • Read the water meter at the same time every day and write it down.

Litter

Litter must be dry and loose. Wet patches under drinkers must be removed and replaced with dry litter. Wet litter makes ammonia, sore feet and disease.

Air and temperature

Check the thermometer and how the birds behave. If you smell strong ammonia or the birds are panting, tell your supervisor. Never change the fans or controller settings unless you are trained and allowed.

Dead and sick birds

Pick up dead birds on every walk. Put them in the dead bird bin. Count them and write the number on the record card. Tell your supervisor about weak, sick or lame birds. Wear gloves and wash your hands after.

Eggs (layer houses)

Collect eggs at the set times. Handle them gently. Keep dirty and cracked eggs separate. Pick up floor eggs. Put eggs in clean trays in the egg room.

lessons.title: Keeping good records
lessons.html:
Keeping good records

Why we write things down

Records tell the supervisor and manager how the birds are doing. They help find problems early. They show how much feed and water the birds use and how many birds died. Without records, nobody knows what is happening in the house.

What to write on the house card

ItemWhen
Dead birds and cullsEvery day, every walk
Water meter readingEvery day at the same time
Feed delivered or usedEach delivery, or daily
Temperature (lowest and highest)Every day
Eggs collected (layers)Every collection
Bird weightsWhen birds are weighed
Vaccines and medicinesEvery time they are given
Problems seenWhen they happen

How to write good records

  • Write the date and the house number.
  • Write clearly with a pen.
  • Write the number straight away. Do not wait until the end of the day.
  • Write only what you counted or saw. Do not guess.
  • If you make a mistake, draw one line through it and write the right number next to it. Do not scratch it out.
  • Sign your name or initials.

Weighing birds

When your supervisor asks, catch birds gently from different places in the house, weigh them one by one on the scale, and write each weight. Set the scale to zero first.

Hand in records

Give your record cards to the supervisor at the time the farm says. Keep the card clean and dry.

Key points

  • Warm the house and have feed and water ready before chicks arrive.
  • Watch chick behaviour to know if they are too hot or too cold.
  • Check feed, water, litter and air on every walk.
  • Pick up and count dead birds every day.
  • Write records straight away, clearly and honestly.
